item.title: How to Hide WhatsApp Chats and Contact Names in Meetings
item.description: Learn how to hide WhatsApp chats, contact names, previews, and profile photos before sharing WhatsApp Web in meetings and demos.
item.content:encoded:
Meetings create a funny kind of privacy problem. You can be careful about the document you intend to present and still expose a private WhatsApp chat in the sidebar. A contact name, profile photo, or last-message preview may be enough for someone to work out what they are looking at.
The fix is to prepare WhatsApp Web before you start sharing, rather than trying to hide things after somebody is already watching. You can blur the chat list, contact names, message previews, and the active conversation separately, then check the whole browser surface like a meeting attendee would.
**Privacy Blur for WhatsApp is a free Chrome extension that blurs chats, messages, names, and media on WhatsApp Web during screen sharing.**
![WhatsApp Web with the full page blurred and Privacy Blur controls open before a meeting](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-full-blurred.png)
## Why chat names are easy to overlook
Most people think about message text first. That makes sense: a message is the obvious private thing on the page. But the left-hand chat list is often more revealing because it stays visible while you navigate. It can show:
- The names of friends, customers, colleagues, or groups - A last-message preview - A profile photo or avatar - A timestamp that gives away when a conversation happened - A group name that reveals a project, client, or personal situation
The active chat header adds another layer. Even if the message area is blurred, the contact or group name may remain readable at the top of the conversation. During a client demo, that can expose an internal project. During a team meeting, it can reveal a private conversation that had nothing to do with the call.
There is also a timing problem. WhatsApp Web can update while you are sharing. A new message may change a preview, a new chat may move to the top of the sidebar, or you may click into a conversation without noticing how much context is visible around it. A useful privacy routine covers the surrounding interface, not just the paragraph you planned to show.
## Open WhatsApp Web before the meeting
Start at [web.whatsapp.com](https://web.whatsapp.com/), and wait for the page to finish loading before you join the call. A WhatsApp blur tool only affects WhatsApp Web, not private documents in another tab, notifications from another app, or a second monitor.
If Privacy Blur is installed, its floating widget appears on the WhatsApp Web page. Open it and look at the individual zones before choosing a sharing surface. The product works locally on WhatsApp Web in the browser; it does not change your desktop or the WhatsApp desktop app.
## Blur the chat list first
The chat list is the part people forget because it is not the main content area. In a meeting, though, it is often sitting at the edge of the shared tab the entire time.
Turn on the chat-list control to blur names in the left sidebar. Then look for anything that could still identify a conversation:
1. Can you recognize a person from a visible avatar? 2. Is the last-message preview readable? 3. Does a group name identify a client or project? 4. Is the top item in the list likely to change when a new message arrives? 5. Does the search field contain a private name or phrase?
If the sidebar is part of the demo, you may prefer to keep its structure visible while hiding the text. If you are presenting a general workflow and do not need the list at all, a broader blur is less distracting.
![WhatsApp chat list and message content blurred while the Privacy Blur panel remains visible](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-messages-blurred.png)
## Hide the active contact or group name
Next, check the header of the conversation you plan to use. The contact-name control hides the current chat title and sender names in the conversation. This matters even when the message text is already blurred: a name can identify the relationship, company, or topic without revealing a single sentence.
Open the conversation you plan to share, enable contact-name blur, and then switch to a safe test chat if you need to confirm the effect. Do not rely on the control label alone. Read the page visually from the position where a meeting participant will see it.
Profile photos deserve a similar check. A familiar face, company logo, or group avatar can identify the chat even if the name is covered. Privacy Blur includes a profile-photo zone for avatars in the sidebar, header, and chat information view.
## Cover previews, not just message bodies
A preview is a short piece of text, but short does not mean harmless. “The contract is signed,” “Can you call me tonight?” or a client’s name can give away more than a long conversation hidden below it.
Enable preview blur when people will see the chat list. You can leave the general layout in place and still remove the words that make each conversation identifiable. This is a good middle ground for a product demo: viewers understand where chats live, but they do not get a readable list of private topics.
If you are sharing a personal WhatsApp account in a public webinar or recording, use the broader setting. The fewer pieces of live personal context on the page, the less you have to monitor while you talk.
## Use the global toggle when time is short
Individual zones are useful when you want a carefully balanced presentation. But meetings do not always give you five quiet minutes. Someone says, “Can you share your WhatsApp workflow?” and suddenly you are choosing a browser tab.
The global toggle gives you a fast first move:
1. Open the Privacy Blur widget. 2. Turn on the global blur state. 3. Select the WhatsApp Web tab or window you intend to share. 4. Check the active header, sidebar, previews, profile photo, and message area. 5. Adjust individual zones only if you need more of the interface to remain readable.
![Privacy Blur for WhatsApp showing independent controls for names, previews, chats, and media](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/privacy-blur-panel.png)
The point is not to make a promise that nothing private can ever appear. The point is to create a safer visual starting state before you click Share.
## Keep the blur on when you change chats
Switching conversations is where a careful setup can fall apart. You may open another chat to demonstrate a feature, click a new item in the sidebar, or search for a contact while the meeting is still running.
Leave the global blur state enabled, then recheck the new page state. Look at:
- The new contact or group header - The chat-list row you selected - Any message preview or media thumbnail - The compose box, especially if you typed a search or draft - Profile photos and other identifying details
WhatsApp Web updates dynamically, so a page that looked safe ten minutes ago is not necessarily the same page after new messages arrive. Privacy Blur is designed to reapply its visual zones as the interface changes, but you should still glance at the shared surface after moving around.
## Reveal one item without removing everything
Sometimes you need to read a detail yourself. You might be checking the exact wording of a test message or confirming which conversation is open. If hover-to-reveal is enabled, move over the blurred area locally instead of switching the whole privacy layer off.
Anyone viewing your shared screen can see an item while it is revealed, so stop sharing before revealing private content. After moving the pointer away, confirm that the page returned to its blurred state. Hover reveal does not make the underlying WhatsApp data private from someone who already has access to the account.
## Meeting examples
### Team standup
For a standup, you may only need to hide personal names and message previews. Keep the WhatsApp layout visible if you are demonstrating a work process, but blur the chat list, contact names, profile photos, and preview text. If the meeting is recorded, add message and media blur too.
### Client demo
A client demo usually needs a cleaner surface. Turn on the global toggle, then open a test conversation or a chat containing dummy content. Hide the sidebar if it includes internal project names, and blur the compose box before typing anything in front of the client.
### Support call
Support calls often involve switching between conversations while explaining a workflow. Use the broad blur state before the call, keep it enabled while navigating, and use hover reveal only when you need to inspect one item. Do not open a customer’s private message simply to prove that blur is working.
### Recorded tutorial
For a tutorial, use a test account or dummy conversation whenever possible. Blur is helpful, but it does not turn real private data into safe demo data. Check the profile photo, chat header, sidebar, media, and notifications before recording, then review the finished recording before publishing it.
## Choose the right Chrome sharing surface
The blur layer protects content inside WhatsApp Web. Chrome’s [screen-sharing guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/avoiding-oversharing-when-screen-sharing/) explains why sharing a specific tab usually exposes less unrelated information than sharing the entire screen.
When your meeting tool offers the choice, prefer the WhatsApp Web tab. If that is not practical, use a browser window containing only the work you intend to show. Share the entire desktop only when you really need to.
This choice and the blur setting solve different problems. Tab sharing reduces unrelated exposure. Visual blur hides selected WhatsApp content inside the tab. You want both habits working together.
## What this protects—and what it does not
Privacy Blur is visual privacy for screen sharing. Its blur operation runs locally on WhatsApp Web, and no WhatsApp message content is sent to Amrita Labs. The product does not collect or transmit your message text, contact names, phone numbers, photos, videos, or chat files for the blur operation. Anonymous product-usage events are separate from WhatsApp content.
That promise is intentionally narrow. The extension does not encrypt WhatsApp messages. It does not protect the underlying page from browser developer tools, and it does not hide another tab, app, device, or desktop surface. It cannot guarantee that a meeting recording contains no private information. You still need to choose the right share target and review what is visible.
The [Privacy Blur for WhatsApp privacy policy](https://amrita-labs.com/privacy-blur-whatsapp/privacy/) explains the local blur behavior, analytics boundary, and payment flow in more detail.
## A repeatable pre-meeting routine
Before your next meeting, try this order:
1. Open WhatsApp Web early. 2. Turn on the global blur state. 3. Blur the chat list and contact names. 4. Add preview, profile-photo, message, and media blur if the meeting is recorded or public. 5. Check the compose box and search field. 6. Select the intended tab or window. 7. Look at the page from a viewer’s perspective. 8. Keep blur enabled while you switch conversations. 9. Stop sharing before opening an unrelated private page.
After a few repetitions, the routine becomes quick. More importantly, it moves the privacy decision to the calm part of the meeting—before you are already presenting.

It gives you independent controls for chats, names, previews, profile photos, messages, media, and the compose box, plus a global toggle when you need to move quickly.

item.title: WhatsApp Web Privacy Checklist for Screen Sharing
item.description: Use this WhatsApp Web privacy checklist before screen sharing in meetings, demos, support calls, and recorded tutorials.
item.content:encoded:
Screen sharing is usually a last-minute action. Someone asks for a demo, you open the right browser window, and you click Share before thinking about everything else inside it. WhatsApp Web makes that risky because the visible page includes more than the message you meant to discuss.
A good privacy check does not need to be complicated. You want a short routine that catches names, previews, profile photos, media, drafts, and the actual sharing target before another person can see them.
**Privacy Blur for WhatsApp is a free Chrome extension that blurs chats, messages, names, and media on WhatsApp Web during screen sharing.**
![WhatsApp Web before privacy blur is applied, with the Privacy Blur widget ready for screen sharing](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-before.png)
## The five-minute WhatsApp Web check
Use the checklist below before a meeting, sales demo, support call, webinar, or recording. You do not have to hide every part of WhatsApp every time. The goal is to make a deliberate choice instead of sharing the default page by accident.
### 1. Open the correct WhatsApp Web page
Start with [web.whatsapp.com](https://web.whatsapp.com/) in Chrome and let the page finish loading. If you have several windows open, identify the one connected to the account you intend to use.
Do not assume that a tab title is enough. Look at the page itself. Confirm that you are in the browser tab you expect, that the correct chat is open, and that no sign-in or connection screen is going to interrupt your presentation.
If you use Privacy Blur, the floating widget appears on WhatsApp Web. Open it before the meeting starts. The extension works locally on WhatsApp Web; it does not modify other websites or hide anything on your desktop.
### 2. Turn on a safe starting state
If you are not sure which parts of WhatsApp will be visible, turn on the global blur toggle first. This gives you a broad visual privacy layer while you decide which zones to leave readable.
Then inspect the page. A broad blur is useful for a rushed meeting, but you may prefer selective controls for a tutorial where viewers need to understand the interface. Privacy Blur has independent zones for messages, contact names, chat-list names, preview text, profile photos, the compose box, images and videos, and Status or About information.
![WhatsApp Web fully blurred with the global Privacy Blur state enabled](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-full-blurred.png)
### 3. Check the chat list
The sidebar can reveal a surprising amount of context. Look for:
- Private names and group names - Last-message previews - Profile photos - Project or customer references - Unread counts and timestamps
If viewers only need to see the main workflow, blur the chat-list names and previews. If the list is part of your explanation, keep the structure visible but hide the identifying text. Do not leave the sidebar unchecked just because your main conversation is safe.
### 4. Check the active conversation header
Read the contact or group name at the top of the active conversation. Then check the avatar beside it. These details can identify a private chat even when the message area is covered.
Enable contact-name blur and profile-photo blur when the identity of the person or group is not relevant to the meeting. This is especially important for client demos, recorded tutorials, and public webinars, where the audience may not know which information was supposed to remain private.
### 5. Check message text and timestamps
Message blur is the obvious step, but do it deliberately. Scroll through the active conversation and check both recent and older message rows. A single readable sentence may reveal a name, phone number, address, price, or private plan.
Also look at timestamps and message status indicators. They may not contain the message itself, but they can still provide context about a person or conversation. You do not need to remove every visual element for every call; you do need to know what remains visible.
### 6. Check previews and search fields
The chat list is not the only place short text appears. Search fields, link previews, quoted replies, and notification-like rows can expose words you were not planning to show.
Before sharing, clear a private search query and blur preview text if the sidebar is visible. If you typed a contact name to find the right conversation, do not leave that name sitting in the search box while you present.
### 7. Check media and profile photos
A photo can identify someone faster than a message. So can a document thumbnail, video frame, company logo, or familiar group avatar.
Look through the active chat for images, videos, files, and media previews. If the meeting does not need them, enable the Images & Videos zone. Add profile-photo blur for avatars in the sidebar, header, and chat information view.
![WhatsApp Web messages and media blurred while the Privacy Blur panel stays available for local controls](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-messages-blurred.png)
### 8. Check the compose box
Draft text is easy to forget because it is not part of the conversation history. If you typed a reply before the call, the compose box may contain the most sensitive line on the page.
Clear the draft or enable compose-box blur. Do this again if you type while sharing. A demonstration can turn into an accidental disclosure when someone sees a private sentence before you send it.
### 9. Check Status and About details
Contact information can remain visible outside the main message area. If you open a chat information drawer, look for Status or About text, phone numbers, and other details that viewers might not need.
Privacy Blur includes a Status / About zone for this kind of content. If the view is route-dependent or not currently open, simply close the drawer or avoid opening it during the meeting. The safest surface is the one you have actually inspected.
### 10. Choose the right sharing target
Chrome’s [screen-sharing guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/avoiding-oversharing-when-screen-sharing/) explains why sharing a tab usually exposes less unrelated information than sharing the entire screen. When your meeting tool allows it, share the specific WhatsApp Web tab.
If tab sharing is not available, use a browser window containing only the intended work. Avoid sharing the whole desktop unless you need to demonstrate something outside the browser. A full-screen share can expose notifications, other applications, bookmarks, and unrelated tabs.
Remember that tab selection and content blur are separate checks. Choosing the right tab does not hide a readable WhatsApp message. Blurring WhatsApp does not protect a private document in another window.
## Match the blur to the meeting
For a team standup, selective blur can keep navigation readable while hiding names, previews, and profile photos. For a client demo, sales call, webinar, or recording, start with the global blur state, use a test conversation or dummy account, and reveal only what supports the explanation. Support calls deserve the broad state while you move between chats because each new header, preview, and media item needs another check.
Selective zones are useful when the interface itself is part of the lesson: hide names while showing buttons, hide previews while demonstrating the list, or hide the compose box before typing. The global toggle is the safer starting point when the meeting is rushed or you are unsure which zones are active. It is not a guarantee; inspect the sidebar, header, media, compose box, and open information drawers before sharing.
## Keep checking after you start sharing
The privacy pass is not finished when the call begins. WhatsApp Web can update as messages arrive, chats move in the list, and you open new views. Keep blur enabled, avoid opening unrelated pages, and look at the shared surface after navigation.
If you use hover reveal, remember that it is for your local view. Reveal only what you need, keep the pointer over that item, and move away when you are done. Do not turn off the whole privacy layer just to read one line.
## Know the limits of visual privacy
Privacy Blur is a visual privacy tool. Its blur operation runs locally on WhatsApp Web, and no WhatsApp message content is sent to Amrita Labs. The extension does not send message text, contact names, phone numbers, photos, videos, or chat files to Amrita Labs for blurring. Anonymous product-usage analytics are separate from WhatsApp content.
Visual blur is not encryption. It does not protect the underlying page from browser developer tools, and it does not hide content in another tab, application, device, or desktop surface. It cannot guarantee that a screenshot or recording contains no private information. Choose the shared surface carefully and review what you show.
You can read the [Privacy Blur for WhatsApp privacy policy](https://amrita-labs.com/privacy-blur-whatsapp/privacy/) for the full explanation of local processing, analytics, and payment-related data.
## Save this short version
Before you click Share:
1. Open the correct WhatsApp Web tab. 2. Turn on global blur or the zones you need. 3. Check the chat list and previews. 4. Check the active name and profile photo. 5. Check messages, media, and the compose box. 6. Clear private search text. 7. Choose a tab or clean browser window. 8. Test the viewer’s perspective. 9. Keep blur enabled while navigating. 10. Stop sharing before opening another private page.
It takes less time than explaining an accidental preview after the meeting.

item.title: How to Blur WhatsApp Media and Profile Photos on Screen
item.description: Learn how to blur WhatsApp photos, videos, media previews, avatars, and profile pictures before screen sharing in Chrome.
item.content:encoded:
Text is not the only thing that can leak during a WhatsApp Web screen share. A profile photo can identify a contact before anyone reads a message. A video thumbnail can show a face, a document, or a private place. Even a small image in the chat list may tell meeting attendees exactly which conversation is open.
That is why a good WhatsApp privacy setup covers the visual details around the message area too. Before sharing, check the sidebar, conversation header, chat information panel, media thumbnails, and any images or videos already loaded in the thread.

## Why photos are easy to underestimate
People tend to classify a photo as harmless when it is small. In practice, recognition does not require much detail. A familiar face, a company logo, a child’s picture, or the background of a room can identify a private conversation immediately.
Media can also reveal information without being opened. WhatsApp Web may show:
- Image thumbnails in a conversation - Video previews and still frames - Profile photos in the chat list - Avatars in the active conversation header - Photos inside the chat information drawer - Document or link previews with recognizable images
The goal is not to make every pixel of WhatsApp unreadable forever. It is to hide the visual context that does not belong in your meeting, recording, or demo while keeping the page usable for you.

Open [web.whatsapp.com](https://web.whatsapp.com/) in Chrome and wait for the page to finish loading. Then choose the conversation you expect to demonstrate and look at it as if you were sitting in the meeting.
If Privacy Blur is installed, open its floating widget. The extension operates locally on WhatsApp Web and gives you separate controls for messages, contact names, chat-list names, previews, profile photos, the compose box, images and videos, and Status or About information.
Do not prepare only the center of the page. The profile photo in the header and the avatar in the sidebar may be more identifying than the message you plan to show.
## Blur profile photos in every visible location
Profile photos can appear in more than one place, depending on the WhatsApp Web view. Check the sidebar, active chat header, and chat information drawer.
Enable the profile-photo zone, then inspect:
1. The avatar beside the active conversation 2. Profile photos beside chats in the left sidebar 3. Group images and company logos 4. Photos shown in contact or chat details 5. Any larger image that appears after opening a profile view
If a photo still feels recognizable, do not assume that a small size makes it safe. Use the broad blur setting or avoid opening that view during the meeting.
![WhatsApp Web fully blurred, including chat context and visual identifiers, before screen sharing](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/whatsapp-full-blurred.png)
Profile-photo blur is particularly useful in a client demo. You can show the structure of the conversation without displaying a customer’s face or a company mark. It also helps in a recorded tutorial, where a tiny avatar may remain visible in the final video long after you have forgotten that it was there.
## Blur images and videos in the conversation
Next, enable the Images & Videos zone. Scroll through the active conversation and look for every visual surface, not only the newest attachment.
Check:
- Inline photos - Video thumbnails - Animated previews - Images in quoted replies - Shared media cards - Link previews with a visual thumbnail - Files or documents that show a preview image
The safest setting depends on your use case. If the meeting is about WhatsApp navigation, keep the page layout visible and blur the actual media. If you are sharing a private account in a public setting, turn on the global blur state and use a test conversation instead.
Do not open a photo just to check whether the blur works while other people are watching. Test the behavior in a safe chat before the call. Then keep the media zone enabled as you move between conversations.
## Use the panel to control the surrounding context
Media blur works best alongside the zones around it. An image may be covered while its caption or chat preview remains readable. A profile photo may be blurred while the contact name identifies the person.
For a stronger visual privacy setup, consider enabling:
- Contact-name blur for the active header - Chat-list blur for sidebar names - Preview blur for last-message snippets - Message blur for captions and surrounding text - Compose-box blur for drafts and replies - Status / About blur in contact details
![Privacy Blur for WhatsApp panel showing separate controls for media, profile photos, messages, names, and previews](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/whatsapp-blur/privacy-blur-panel.png)
You do not have to use every zone. Selective blur is useful when you need to explain the interface. The important thing is to check the relationship between the image and the text around it.
## Check new media after WhatsApp updates the page
WhatsApp Web is a live interface. New messages can arrive, chats can move in the sidebar, and the page can render additional media after you scroll or open a conversation.
Keep the media blur enabled while sharing. After switching chats, take a quick look at the new header, sidebar, and conversation. If a meeting participant asks you to open another thread, pause before clicking and confirm that the privacy layer is still active.
Privacy Blur is designed to reapply its visual zones as the page changes, but no browser tool removes the need for a quick visual check. Your workflow matters as much as the toggle.
## Hover to reveal only what you need
Sometimes you need to identify a thumbnail or check whether a test image loaded correctly. If hover-to-reveal is enabled, hover over the blurred item locally rather than disabling all media blur.
This is useful when you are working alone or preparing a demo. During a live meeting, keep it brief. Reveal one item, inspect it, and move the pointer away so the page returns to its blurred state. The audience should continue seeing the rest of the content covered.
Hover reveal is a local viewing convenience, not a security boundary. It does not encrypt the original WhatsApp content or prevent someone with access to the account from viewing it somewhere else.
## A safe workflow for common situations
### Client presentation
Use a conversation containing dummy images or a test account if you can. Turn on profile-photo and media blur before selecting the browser tab. Add contact-name and preview blur so the client cannot identify unrelated chats in the sidebar.
### Team meeting
You may only need to cover personal photos and avatars. Keep the general WhatsApp layout readable, but blur profile photos, chat-list names, and media thumbnails. If the meeting is recorded, use message blur as well.
### Support or troubleshooting call
Support work often requires opening several conversations. Start with the global toggle, then keep media and profile-photo blur enabled while navigating. Stop sharing before using hover reveal or changing privacy settings to inspect a private image.
### Tutorial or webinar
Assume the recording can be replayed and downloaded. Use dummy content, blur all visible media, and test a short capture before recording the full session. A visual layer can reduce accidental exposure, but it cannot turn real private photos into safe teaching material.

## Test the viewer’s perspective
Your own screen is not always a good approximation of what other people see. Before the meeting, zoom out to the size a participant might receive, or join from another device and look at the shared view.
Ask:
- Can I recognize the profile photo? - Is a company logo still visible? - Can I identify a group from its avatar? - Is a media thumbnail understandable even while blurred? - Does a caption explain what the image contains? - Are any visual previews visible in the sidebar? - Did I select the intended Chrome tab?

item.title: How to Choose the Right Pinterest Board for Every Pin
item.description: A practical way to choose the right Pinterest board for a Pin, with examples for Etsy sellers, bloggers, and product creators.
item.content:encoded:
Choosing a Pinterest board can feel like a tiny dropdown decision. It usually happens at the end of the publishing process, when the image is finished, the copy is written, and you’re ready to move on. That’s exactly when it’s easy to choose the first board that seems vaguely related.
The better question is simpler: **What would someone expect to find on this board, and does this Pin belong in that collection?**
Pinello is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time.
That score is a pre-publish quality review, not a reach forecast. Board fit is a context decision you can inspect before publishing, while the draft is still easy to change.
![Pinello Pin Doctor reviewing a Pinterest draft with board context and a focused next action](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/etsy-pin-doctor.png)
## What Pinterest says a board is for
Pinterest describes boards as collections for your Pins. Its official create-a-board guidance asks you to give the board a name and lets you keep it secret or add collaborators. Pinterest’s business guidance also recommends organizing Pins into well-named boards, with examples such as “Easy No-bake Dinners.”
That advice points to a useful standard: a board name should help someone understand the subject of the collection. It doesn’t need to sound clever. It needs to be clear enough that a new Pin can be judged against it.
This is also why a board is more than a storage folder. It gives the Pin a little context. The same image can feel perfectly placed on “Small Apartment Storage” and oddly broad on “Home Ideas,” even if both boards are technically related.
## Start with the Pin’s promise
Before looking at your board list, describe the Pin in one sentence.
> This Pin shows three printable chore charts for families with young children.
Or:
> This Pin presents a handmade ceramic mug as a cozy gift for coffee lovers.
That sentence is your board brief. It tells you what the Pin is about, who it is for, and why someone might save it. A broad label such as “home,” “gifts,” or “ideas” is much less useful.
Now compare the sentence with your board names. “Printable Kids Activities” gives the first example a clear home. “Fun Stuff” does not. “Personalized Gifts” gives the mug a stronger context than “Things I Make,” unless the Pin is specifically about the making process.
## Five questions that make board choice easier
### 1. Does the board name describe the main topic?
Read the board name and Pin title together. Do they sound like they belong in the same conversation?
“Easy Vegetarian Dinner Recipes” and “30-Minute Lentil Pasta” are naturally connected. “Food Inspiration” is not wrong, but it gives the Pin less specific context.
Specific does not mean stuffing every possible keyword into a board name. It means a visitor can predict the kind of content they’ll find there.
### 2. Does the board match the reason someone would save the Pin?
A wedding invitation template could fit “Wedding Stationery” or “Wedding Planning.” The best choice depends on what the Pin leads with. If the image showcases the design, stationery may be the stronger fit. If it explains how to plan the event, wedding planning may make more sense.
The board should match the Pin’s primary job, not just one word that appears somewhere in the description.
### 3. Would the Pin look natural beside the existing Pins?
Open the board and scan a few neighboring Pins. Are they about the same general subject? Do they serve a similar audience? Would your new Pin look like a normal addition rather than a random exception?
The Pins do not need to be identical. A home decor board can include different rooms and styles. But there should be a reason the collection exists.
This check catches a common problem: a board name sounds relevant, but the actual collection has drifted. A Pin about a printable classroom schedule may technically relate to “Teachers,” while the board itself is filled with teacher outfits and classroom decor. The audience overlap is real, but the content expectation is different.
### 4. Is there a more focused board that honestly fits?
Broad boards are not automatically bad. They can be useful for a large content system or a newer account with fewer collections. Still, if you have a focused board that genuinely matches the Pin, compare the two.
“Recipes” is broad. “Quick Weeknight Dinner Recipes” gives a 30-minute meal more useful context. “Wall Art” describes an item category. “Neutral Nursery Wall Art” describes the category and the use case.
Don’t force a Pin into a narrow board just because the name contains a desirable phrase. If the board doesn’t fit the actual content, the specificity becomes misleading.
### 5. Can you explain the choice in one sentence?
Try this:
> I’m saving this Pin to [board] because it helps people who want [topic or outcome].
If that sentence sounds natural, the choice is probably defensible. If it turns into a paragraph of excuses, pause. A different board may fit better, or the Pin itself may need a clearer promise.
## Board fit examples
### Etsy sellers
Imagine a Pin for a personalized birth flower necklace. Possible boards include “Jewelry Ideas,” “Personalized Gifts,” and “Mother’s Day Gifts.”
If the title is “Personalized Birth Flower Necklace Gift,” the personalized-gifts board is a strong primary fit. A Mother’s Day board could also be reasonable when the image and copy actually speak to that occasion. Don’t choose a seasonal board only because the calendar is nearby.
The product, image, title, description, and board should tell the same story. If the board says “Mother’s Day Gifts” but the Pin never mentions the occasion, review whether that context is really part of the draft.
### Bloggers
A post called “Small Balcony Garden Ideas for Renters” could fit “Apartment Gardening,” “Small Space Ideas,” or “Container Gardening.”
Look at what the article teaches. If most of the post is about choosing pots and plants, container gardening may be the most honest home. If it focuses on making a rental balcony usable, small-space ideas may be more natural.
The right board is the one that makes the destination easier to understand, not merely the one with the biggest audience in your account.
### Print-on-demand creators
A funny librarian mug may fit “Mugs,” “Funny Gift Ideas,” or “Librarian Gifts.” When the title and image speak directly to librarians, the audience-specific board gives the Pin clearer context.
On the other hand, a Pin about the design process may belong on an illustration or typography board. The finished product and the behind-the-scenes process are different promises, even when they involve the same artwork.
## When two boards both make sense
Board fit is not always binary. A meal-planning checklist may honestly belong on “Meal Planning” and “Organization Printables.” A nursery print may fit “Nursery Decor” and “Baby Shower Gifts.”
When that happens, use the destination and the Pin’s lead message to decide:
1. What does the image show first? 2. What does the title name first? 3. What would the reader find after clicking? 4. Which board would make the Pin easiest to understand?
You don’t need to pretend there is one mathematically correct answer. Choose the most defensible context, then keep the copy aligned with that choice.
## Use Board Match as a second opinion
When you have a short list, select the board in the Create Pin workflow and run **Board Match** in Pinello. It is an explicit, user-triggered check—not a background claim about Pinterest’s ranking system.
Board Match is useful when two board names are close, the Pin’s audience changed during editing, or you’re publishing several related drafts and want a consistent review step. Read the result alongside the board itself. If it points to a mismatch, inspect the title, description, topics, and neighboring Pins before changing anything.
The result may indicate that the board is wrong. It may also reveal that the Pin copy is too broad. And sometimes both boards are reasonable and your judgment should decide. Board Match is a recommendation, not an official Pinterest label, endorsement, or promise of distribution.
![Pinello Pin Doctor showing a board-related review state for a Pinterest draft](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-before.png)
## Fix the mismatch instead of hiding it
If the board doesn’t fit, you have more than one repair option:
- choose a board that matches the existing Pin - rewrite the title so the actual topic is clearer - add useful context to the description - change the image when it is making a different promise - create a new board only when the topic is real and repeatable for your account
Changing the board without rereading the copy is a surprisingly easy mistake. A Pin can look right in the new collection while still carrying wording from the old one.
Likewise, changing the title may change the best board. A Pin called “Neutral Nursery Decor” has a different context from the same image titled “Baby Shower Gift Ideas.” The board should follow the final promise, not the first draft.
![Pinello Pin Doctor after a Pinterest Pin copy and context repair](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-after.png)
## A quick pre-publish board review
Read these together:
- the image - the title - the description and available topics or hashtags - the selected board - the destination page
If they all point toward the same subject, the board is probably doing its job. If one item feels like it belongs to a different Pin, fix the clearest mismatch first.
This review cannot tell you what Pinterest will do after publication. It can help you avoid publishing a Pin that is confusing, incomplete, or sitting in an unrelated collection.
## Make board fit part of your workflow
[Use Pinello’s pre-publish board and Pin Doctor review](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=pinello_pre_publish) when you want a second set of eyes beside the Create Pin form. AI actions are copy-only and user-triggered: Pinello copies a suggestion for you to review, but it never types into Pinterest or publishes for you.

item.title: Pinterest Image Quality Checklist: Size, Ratio, and Readability Before Posting
item.description: Review Pinterest image size, ratio, resolution, format, contrast, and mobile readability before posting a Pin.
item.content:encoded:
A beautiful Pin can still be difficult to use if the crop is strange, the headline disappears at thumbnail size, or the source file is too soft to inspect.
That’s why image quality belongs in the workflow before the title and description are finished. An Etsy seller needs the product to be visible. A blogger needs the graphic to explain the article during a quick scroll. A print-on-demand creator needs enough contrast that the design doesn’t turn into a fuzzy block of color.
This is not about chasing one perfect Pinterest image size. It’s about catching avoidable problems while the source file is still easy to change.
Pinello is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time.
The image dimension is a pre-publish quality review. It can flag practical issues, but it cannot promise impressions, saves, clicks, ranking, or future performance.
![Pinello Pin Doctor reviewing a Pinterest draft with image and copy checks](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/etsy-pin-doctor.png)
## Start with the ratio, but don’t worship it
Vertical images are a practical default on Pinterest because they use more of the feed’s visual space. Many creators work with a **2:3 ratio**, often **1000 × 1500 pixels**, for a standard Pin graphic. Pinterest’s creative guidance uses 2:3 for standard image creative, especially in its advertising specifications.
Treat that as a useful starting point, not a universal organic requirement. The important part is the relationship between width and height. A large file can still have an awkward shape. A square image can be sharp and intentional while giving you less room for a headline, product detail, or visual explanation.
Before posting, ask:
- Is the canvas intentionally shaped for this Pin? - Will the important subject survive the crop? - Is the headline or product label inside a safe area? - Does the image make sense without the design file open beside it?
Pinterest’s Pin specification guide also provides safe-zone measurements for keeping text and other elements visible across devices. It lists 270 px at the top, 65 px on the left, 195 px on the right, and 790 px at the bottom. Those measurements are useful when you’re placing important text, especially on a tall canvas.
## Check pixel dimensions and resolution
Pixel dimensions tell you how large the file is. Resolution is how clear the important details look at the size people actually see.
A low-resolution image may look acceptable inside a design tool and become visibly soft when Pinterest displays it in a larger context. For a blog graphic, inspect small text and thin lines. For an Etsy product image, zoom in on edges, texture, and labels. For a POD mockup, check the printed area rather than only the background.
Don’t resize a tiny source file upward and assume the problem is solved. Upscaling can make the file bigger without restoring detail. If the original is blurry, return to the design or product photo when possible.
Pinterest lists several common image file types, with a 20 MB maximum for web uploads in its Pin specification guide. Use the format that preserves your image cleanly and fits your workflow. PNG is often a sensible choice for graphics with text and sharp edges; JPEG can be practical for photographs.
![A Pinterest Pin Doctor draft before an image and copy repair](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-before.png)
## Test the image at feed size
The desktop editor is generous. Pinterest feeds are not.
Zoom the image out until it is roughly the size of a feed card, or look at it on a smaller screen. Can you identify the topic in a second? Can you read the headline without leaning toward the screen? Do you notice the product or the background decoration first?
Try this quick test:
1. Look at the image for one second. 2. Say what it is about. 3. Read the main text without zooming. 4. Notice where your eye lands first.
If the answer is “I can tell it’s a graphic, but I don’t know what it offers,” the design needs a clearer focal point. If you can read the words only after zooming, the words are not doing useful work in the feed.
This is where many polished designs fail. They look great in the editor because the editor is large. The Pin itself may be competing with dozens of other images in a narrow column.
The one-second test is also useful for product photography. If the first thing you notice is a prop, shadow, or decorative frame, ask whether that is actually what you want the viewer to remember. A clean background often beats a more elaborate scene when the product is the point.
For a blog graphic, try hiding the destination title and looking only at the image. Can you tell whether it is a recipe, tutorial, checklist, or opinion piece? If not, the image may be relying too heavily on metadata that a viewer will not see immediately.
## Keep text readable without making the image noisy
Text overlays can help a Pin explain itself, but too much text turns an image into a poster nobody wants to read while scrolling.
Use one clear headline and, if needed, a short supporting line. Give the type enough contrast from the background. A dark photo with a thin gray font is a problem even when the file technically has excellent resolution.
Watch for:
- low contrast between text and image - decorative fonts that collapse at small sizes - long headlines broken across too many lines - text touching the edge of the canvas - product details hidden behind stickers or badges - several competing calls to action
For an Etsy listing, the product should remain the visual anchor. For a recipe blog, the finished dish should not disappear behind six lines of copy. For a POD Pin, show enough of the design that the buyer does not have to guess what is being sold.
If the image needs a paragraph of explanation before it makes sense, simplify the image or make the title carry a clearer part of the promise.
## Make the image agree with the Pin
Image quality is not isolated from the rest of the draft. If the image says “beginner watercolor supplies” but the title says “advanced painting techniques,” the Pin gives mixed signals to a human reader.
Read the package together:
- **Image:** shows the subject clearly - **Title:** names the primary topic - **Description:** adds useful context - **Topics or hashtags:** support the subject - **Board:** is an honest fit - **Destination:** delivers what the Pin says it will deliver
Pinterest’s business guidance describes Pins as content that can link directly to a site, and recommends adding a URL when you want to drive traffic back to that site. That makes destination alignment part of image quality too. A strong graphic that leads to an unrelated page is still a weak publishing package.
Pinello’s Pin Doctor reviews these areas together. Its SEO Audit and Board Match checks can help you find a mismatch, but they do not measure audience demand or predict whether a Pin will perform.
![Pinterest Pin Doctor after the draft has clearer image context and revised copy](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/room-ideas-after.png)
## A practical image review before upload
Run through these checks before you leave the Create Pin screen:
**Ratio:** Is the canvas intentionally vertical, commonly 2:3 when that suits the design?
**Size:** Is it large enough for the details you need to show?
**Resolution:** Does the source look crisp at feed and close-up sizes?
**Format:** Is it a supported file type that your workflow and Pinterest upload handle cleanly?
**Safe placement:** Are important words, labels, and subjects away from the edges?
**Readability:** Can the headline be read on a phone?
**Contrast:** Does the text stand out without harsh effects that damage the image?
**Focus:** Is there one obvious subject?
**Alignment:** Do the image, title, description, topics, board, and destination describe the same thing?
The list is deliberately boring. Boring checks catch more real problems than another round of decorative tweaks.
One last practical detail: look at the image after exporting it, not only inside Canva, Figma, Photoshop, or your design tool. Export settings can change sharpness, color, and compression. A headline that looked crisp in the source file may soften after export, and a subtle background may become muddy. Open the actual file you plan to upload and inspect that version.
If you are making several variations, compare them at the same display size. Otherwise the largest preview usually wins simply because it is easier to inspect. The question is not which file looks most impressive at full resolution. It is which version stays clear when the Pin is small.
## What Pinello can and cannot tell you
Pinello can inspect image ratio, resolution, format, and text-overlay density locally. It can combine those checks with title, description, topics, board, and SEO checks in the Pin Doctor.
It cannot tell you that a particular size will produce a certain number of saves, clicks, impressions, or rankings. It does not predict future performance, and it is not an official Pinterest quality grade. The score is Pinello’s heuristic summary of the information available in the draft.
That makes it most useful before publishing, when you can still replace the image, shorten the headline, or choose a better board.
If you use an AI action for copy, it is user-triggered and copy-only. Pinello gives you text to review and copy; it does not type into Pinterest or publish for you.
[Review your next Pin with Pinello before you publish](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=pinello_pre_publish).

item.title: How to Save, Sort, and Export Pinterest Pins for Later
item.description: Build a practical Pinterest reference workflow: save Pins to boards, sort what you collect, and export your own research without confusing it with Pinterest Analytics.
item.content:encoded:
Saving a Pinterest Pin takes a second. Finding the useful one again can take much longer.
That is why a good save workflow needs more than a growing collection of boards. You need a reason for saving, a way to narrow the list later, and an export path when your own research needs to leave the browser.
Pinterest already provides the basic save and board tools. Pinello adds a local Favorites workflow for creators who want to keep scored and unscored examples nearby while they browse. The two systems serve different jobs: Pinterest is the place where Pins and boards live; Pinello is a private working list for inspection and pre-publish research.
Pinello is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time.
## 1. Save a Pin to a Pinterest board
Pinterest's official Help Center describes the normal desktop flow: hover over a Pin or open it in closeup, select the save control, and choose a board. You can also create a new board from the save flow. On mobile, open the Pin, tap Save, and select an existing or new board.
Start by choosing the board that best describes the Pin's subject, not merely the board you opened most recently. If you are collecting examples for a product launch, “small bedroom storage” is more useful than a broad “ideas” board. If you are saving recipe references, a board organized around the meal or audience may be easier to revisit than one named only “food.”
Boards are public or private depending on your settings and purpose. A private board can be useful for early research, drafts, or ideas you are not ready to share. A collaborative board has a different purpose: it lets invited people contribute. Decide which kind of collection you are building before you fill it.
![Pinterest Pinello Favorites showing a local collection of saved Pins with thumbnails, titles, and scores.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/sidepanel/favourites.png)
Saving a Pin to Pinterest does not download the image to your computer. It keeps the Pin in a board so you can find it on Pinterest later.
## 2. Give every save a reason
The fastest way to make a board noisy is to save everything that looks vaguely relevant.
Before saving, finish this sentence:
> I am saving this because…
Useful answers include:
- the image makes the product understandable at thumbnail size - the title names a specific audience or problem - the board is tightly focused - the description adds useful context - the Pin is a good reference for a format you want to test - the destination page matches the promise of the Pin
This habit separates inspiration from research. A mood board can be broad and emotional. A working library should help you make a decision later.
Also save a few imperfect examples. A Pin with a strong image and a vague title can teach you where the draft loses clarity. A Pin with an interesting topic but a weak board match can show you what to check before you publish. If you save only polished references, your collection may look good while giving you fewer practical comparisons.
## 3. Sort your Pinterest boards
Pinterest's official board-organization guide explains that boards can be sorted automatically by options such as A to Z, Custom, or Last saved to. On desktop, you can also drag boards into a custom order. Mobile offers comparable sorting and drag-and-drop controls.
Use board order to reflect your current work, not an imaginary permanent taxonomy. Put active projects or current seasonal topics where you can reach them quickly. Move archive boards lower. If you have boards for clients or shops, group them in a way that reduces accidental saves to the wrong place.
Board order is not the same as Pin order. A tidy profile does not automatically make every board useful. Review the board name, description, sections, and recent saves as separate pieces of organization.
Pinterest may also show unorganized ideas that can be reviewed or moved. Treat that area as a queue, not a final library. A Pin that stays unclassified for months is harder to use when you need it.
## 4. Use Pinello Favorites for the working shortlist
Pinterest boards are good for keeping a Pin in its platform context. Pinello Favorites are useful when you want a smaller local shortlist while you inspect examples and prepare your own draft.
From the feed or Pin detail view, you can save a Pin to Favorites. Pinello can keep the Pin URL, thumbnail, title, board information, saved date, and available score context. A Pin can be useful even when Pinterest does not expose enough data for a complete score, so unscored references should not be discarded automatically.
![Pinello Favorites filter view, with score sorting that helps narrow a larger local research list.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/sidepanel/favourites-filter.png)
Sort by score when you need to review the strongest matches to Pinello's checks first. Sort by title when you are looking for a topic. Filter the list to reduce a large collection to the few Pins relevant to the draft in front of you.
Do not treat the score as a creative verdict. A low-scoring Pin may contain a useful composition or product idea. A high-scoring Pin may be irrelevant to your audience. Use the score to choose what to inspect next, then read the Pin yourself.
Pinello Favorites are local to the browser profile. They are not a Pinterest backup service, and they are not a shared team database. If you clear local extension data or uninstall the extension, local records may no longer be available. Export your own data when you need a separate copy.
## 5. Know the difference between save, download, and export
These three actions are often confused:
**Save** keeps a Pin on a Pinterest board so you can find it on Pinterest.
**Download** saves an available image file to your device. Pinterest's official download guide says to use the ellipsis menu and choose Download image. Not every Pin has the option, and Pinterest currently does not offer a separate original-resolution download for every image. Video Pins have different limitations.
**Export** creates a structured copy of information for use elsewhere, such as a CSV for your own spreadsheet.
Downloading an image is not the same as exporting a board. Pinterest's official help pages document saving and individual image downloads, but they do not promise a universal one-click export of every board and every metadata field. Be cautious with third-party downloaders: check permissions, privacy policies, licensing, and the current Pinterest rules before using one.
![Pinello side panel with a Pin detail view, useful when you want to inspect a reference before saving it to your local shortlist.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/sidepanel/side-panel.png)
## 6. Export your own Pinello research
If you use Pinello Pro, CSV export can move scored Pins and Favorites into a spreadsheet. That is useful for a personal research log, a content planning sheet, or a list of references to review with a collaborator.
Think of the CSV as your local record, not as Pinterest Analytics. It may include the information Pinello could verify or store at the time you saved the Pin. It does not add impressions, outbound clicks, conversions, or account-level performance that Pinterest has not provided.
A simple spreadsheet structure can include:
| Column | Why keep it | |---|---| | Pin URL | Return to the original Pin | | Saved date | Remember when you collected it | | Topic | Group the research question | | Board | Preserve the visible context | | Pinello score | Narrow a review list | | Observation | Record what you learned | | Test idea | Turn research into your own next step |
Add your own notes after exporting. “Clear product in first frame” is more useful than “high score.” “Board matches exact customer problem” is more useful than “popular.” Your notes should describe what you can verify, not what you assume caused the Pin's response.
## 7. Make a weekly cleanup routine
A useful library does not need to be enormous.
Once a week, open your Pinterest boards or Pinello Favorites and remove duplicates, irrelevant references, and Pins you no longer understand. Then choose three examples and write one sentence for each:
1. What is clear in the image? 2. What is clear or unclear in the title and description? 3. What would I test differently in my own Pin?
If you publish for several products, use separate board or spreadsheet areas for each audience. Mixing every topic into one research list makes the save count feel productive while making the actual review slower.
## 8. Use the library before publishing
When you are ready to create a Pin, search your saved examples for patterns rather than copying a design.
Look for repeated choices:
- Are titles direct, descriptive, or question-led? - Do boards use a narrow topic or a broad category? - Is the product shown alone, in context, or as a step-by-step? - Do descriptions explain the destination? - Are topics and hashtags related to the same central idea?
Then open Create Pin and review your own draft. Pinello's Pin Doctor checks the image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags or topics. If you use an AI action, it is user-triggered and copy-only. You review the wording and choose whether to paste it; Pinello does not fill fields or publish automatically.
The purpose is not to recreate another creator's Pin. It is to make your own draft easier to understand and easier for you to review.
## A practical setup
Use Pinterest boards for durable platform organization. Use Pinello Favorites for a local working shortlist. Use a CSV export when you need your own records in a spreadsheet. Use Pinterest Analytics after publishing when you need observed account or Pin results.
That division keeps each tool honest. A saved Pin is a reference. A downloaded image is a local file whose rights and context still matter. A CSV is your research record. Analytics is measurement. None of these is a guarantee of reach or ranking.
For a browser-side shortlist that stays close to your Pin workflow, [try Pinello](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=save-sort-export-pins). Save references, narrow them with local sorting and filtering, and review your next draft before publishing.
## Sources
- [Save Pins to a board](https://help.pinterest.com/en/article/save-pins-on-pinterest) - [Organize your boards](https://help.pinterest.com/en/article/organize-your-boards) - [Download an image from a Pin](https://help.pinterest.com/en/article/download-an-image) - [Pinterest analytics explained: tools, metrics, insights](https://create.pinterest.com/blog/pinterest-analytics-explained-tools-metrics-insights/)

item.title: How Pinterest Pin Scoring Works While You Browse
item.description: Learn what Pinello checks on Pinterest feed cards and Pin detail pages, why scores can change, and how to use a browsing score without treating it as a reach prediction.
item.content:encoded:
Pinterest is built for browsing. You can move from a search result to a board to a closeup Pin in a few seconds, often before you know whether a reference is worth saving.
That is where an in-feed score can help. It gives you a quick reason to pause and inspect a Pin. It should not turn browsing into a leaderboard or pretend to know what Pinterest will distribute next.
Pinello adds a Feed Score to Pin cards and a fuller Pin Detail Score when you open a Pin. Both are inspection signals based on the information available at that surface. They help you decide what to look at next and what to learn from a reference.
Pinello is a free Chrome extension that scores Pinterest pins across 5 dimensions — image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags — in real time.
## What “while you browse” means
The feed is a quick context. Pinterest may expose a thumbnail, title, board, creator, and some engagement information without loading every field associated with the Pin. A browser-side tool has to work with what is visible and available at that moment.
Pinello's Feed Score is designed for that context. It can appear on a Pin card or become more visible when you hover, depending on the page state. You can scan several cards, notice a Pin that deserves attention, and open the one that is most relevant to your question.
![Pinello Feed Score badges visible on Pinterest cards while browsing.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/feed/feed-score.png)
The score is not a Pinterest-owned metric. It is not the Pinterest ranking algorithm, a distribution forecast, or a measure of guaranteed reach. It is Pinello's own signal from the available content and context.
## The five dimensions behind the workflow
The same five areas matter when you are inspecting a reference and when you are checking your own draft:
**Image.** Can you understand the subject quickly? Is the main object visible? Does the layout remain legible as a small feed card? A visually attractive image can still be difficult to interpret when reduced.
**Board fit.** Does the Pin seem at home on the board where it appears? A board name can give useful context, but related words are not the same as a precise match. Fit is a relevance check, not a claim about ranking.
**Title.** Does the title tell you the topic, audience, use case, or benefit? Vague language can make a good idea harder to understand. Clear language does not guarantee a click, but it gives the reader a better starting point.
**Description.** Does the description add context and connect naturally to the destination? Repeating a title without explanation may leave the Pin under-specified. More words are not automatically better; useful words are better.
**Hashtags or topics.** Are the terms related to the actual subject? A long list of unrelated terms can create noise. A short set of relevant topics can make the Pin easier to interpret.
Not every Pin exposes every field. If data is missing, the score may be limited or unavailable. A missing value is not proof that the Pin has no title, no board, or no engagement. It can simply mean the current page did not make that information verifiable.
## Why the Feed Score can change
You may see one score on a feed card and another after opening the Pin. That is expected.
The feed is optimized for quick discovery. The closeup page can expose fuller information, including a longer title or description, board details, image dimensions, creator context, and more available stats. When more inputs are available, Pinello can make a more complete Pin Detail Score.
![Pinello feed and detail comparison showing how a fuller Pin view provides additional context for inspection.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-details/feed-score-comparison-with-pin-detail-1.png)
The change does not mean the Pin suddenly became better or worse. It means the inspection changed. Treat the feed score as a filter for attention and the detail score as a closer review.
This is similar to reading a book cover before opening the book. The cover helps you decide whether to look closer. The inside pages give you more information. They are related checks, not identical evidence.
## Use the score to choose what to inspect
A useful browsing routine is simple:
1. Scan the feed normally. 2. Notice a score that makes a Pin worth opening, not a score that tells you to copy it. 3. Open the Pin and read the available title, description, board, and destination. 4. Look at the creator and board context when it is available. 5. Save the reference if it answers a question for your own work.
The question is not “Which Pin wins?” It is “Which Pin can teach me something I can verify?”
Maybe the image makes a product obvious in a small card. Maybe the board title is unusually specific. Maybe the description explains what happens after the click. Maybe the Pin is a useful example precisely because one field is weak.
Pinello Favorites can keep those references local. You can save scored or unscored Pins, then sort or filter the list when you are ready to review a smaller set.
![Pinello side panel with a Pin detail view and context for deciding whether to save a reference.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/sidepanel/side-panel.png)
## What the score can tell you
The score can tell you how closely a Pin matches Pinello's checks using the current available data.
It can help you:
- find references with clear or complete fields - identify Pins worth opening in detail - notice repeated metadata patterns in a topic - compare a few examples before drafting your own Pin - decide where a pre-publish review should begin
It can also help you notice uncertainty. A score with missing inputs deserves a different reading from a score based on a fuller Pin view. If the interface shows an unavailable field, leave it unavailable rather than filling the gap with a guess.
## What the score cannot tell you
It cannot tell you that a Pin will rank, go viral, earn a specific number of saves, or drive traffic to your site. It cannot reveal every impression, audience segment, conversion, or distribution decision Pinterest has made.
Pinterest Analytics is the right place to measure your own account and published Pins. Pinterest's official guidance describes metrics such as impressions, saves, Pin clicks, outbound clicks, total audience, and engaged audience. Those measurements belong to your account, your date range, and your tracking setup. A public Pin's visible score is not a substitute for them.
It also cannot tell you why a Pin performed. If a Pin has many saves, the image may have helped, but topic demand, timing, account context, and audience can matter too. Use the score and visible stats to form a question, not a causal conclusion.
## Score the draft where changes are still possible
Browsing is useful for collecting patterns. The most actionable check happens in Create Pin.
Pin Doctor reviews the image, board fit, title, description, and hashtags or topics on your draft. It can highlight a focus issue so you have a clear next action rather than a wall of warnings. After you revise, review the result again.
If you request an AI action, it remains user-triggered and copy-only. Pinello can suggest a title, description, or topics and place the text on your clipboard. You decide whether the wording is accurate and on-brand, then paste it yourself. Pinello does not type into Pinterest fields or publish automatically.
![Pinello Pin Doctor with a focused pre-publish issue, showing the difference between browsing a reference and reviewing your own draft.](https://amrita-labs.com/assets/blog/pinello/pin-doctor/title-description-expanded.png)
This is the useful handoff: browse for examples, inspect context, save what teaches you something, then improve your own controllable fields before publishing.
## A five-minute browsing exercise
Choose a single search topic rather than scrolling without a question.
First, scan ten or so Pins and note which images are understandable without opening them. Do not rank them by score alone.
Next, open three Pins with different strengths. Read the title, description, board, and destination. Notice whether the metadata supports the image.
Then save one strong example and one imperfect example to Favorites. Write a short observation for each. “Product is visible immediately” is useful. “This will go viral” is not verifiable.
Finally, open Create Pin and review your own draft with the same five dimensions. The goal is not to imitate the references. It is to make the subject, context, and destination easier to understand.
## Browse with realistic expectations
An in-feed score should reduce friction, not create false certainty. Use it as a second set of eyes while you discover ideas. Open the detail view when context matters. Save examples you can learn from. Check your own draft before publishing. Measure your own results afterward with Pinterest Analytics.
That sequence respects what each tool can know.
If you want a browsing score that leads into a pre-publish review, [try Pinello](https://amrita-labs.com/pinello/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=pinterest-scoring-while-browsing). It helps you inspect the Pin in front of you without promising reach, ranking, or virality.
